newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy reaches agreement on TV soccer rights.
newsitem.headline: Italy reaches agreement on TV soccer rights.

text.p: Soccer authorities agreed on Tuesday to a deal between Italy's main broadcasters to end more than a year of disputes over who should televise the nations's favourite sport.

The Milan-based soccer league voted in favour of an agreement signed on Monday to carve up rights to broadcast soccer and put an end to a long-running dispute between media tycoon Vittorio Cecchi Gori and public broadcaster RAI.
The league said 26 cup matches would be divided up over two years between Cecchi Gori's TeleMonteCarlo (TMC), RAI and Mediaset, owned by centre-right politician Silvio Berlusconi.
"In the cup the (Italian soccer) league will make 26 games available, instead of 13 last year, of which 11 will be shown by RAI, 9 by Mediaset and 6 by TMC," league president Franco Carraro said.
Cecchi Gori will show the first three rounds of the cup, with other matches and the final going to the other two parties.
Under the agreement, the stations would pay 46 billion lire ($27 million) to the league over two years for the rights to show the cup in the 1997/98 and 1998/99 seasons, Carraro said.
RAI will maintain exclusive live radio and recorded TV rights to Italian league matches under an old agreement, with TMC screening serie A games during evening prime time.
"I think the solution... satifies all three parties who fought for the television rights last year," Carraro said.

"The agreement is intelligent and satisfying," Massimo Moratti, chairman of Milan club Internazionale, said. "The most important thing is it brought an end to the disagreement between the various broadcasters."
Cecchi Gori was awarded soccer TV and radio rights in February last year after he offered the soccer league 213.5 billion lire a year for exclusive coverage.
RAI offered only 185 billion lire in the secret auction and the prospect of losing the rights, which it has always held, sent shock waves through the company.
The two broadcasters and Mediaset have since been involved in a complex series of arguments and court hearings, settled by this week's deal.

The deal does not cover pay-per-view screening of Italian league soccer, broadcast in coded form, which belong to the Telepiu-2 channel. Neither does it cover matches played by the national team or European club competitions.
